Uttermost
UT-ur-mohst
adj., n.
Superlative of utter (Old English ūtera, outer), from ūt, out. Webster 1828: extreme; being in the furthest, greatest or highest degree. The Authorized Version uses it two ways — of distance, the uttermost part of the earth, and of degree, saved to the uttermost. The second is where the gospel lives.

Biblical Definition

Uttermost is the Authorized Version’s word for the far edge — of the map, or of the case. Geographically it marks the end of the known world: Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession (Psalm 2:8), and the risen Christ sends His witnesses unto the uttermost part of the earth (Acts 1:8). Morally it marks the limit of endurance under wrath: the wrath is come upon them to the uttermost (1 Thessalonians 2:16). But the word’s whole weight rests on one verse: Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them (Hebrews 7:25). The Greek there is pantelēs — completely, to the very end, with nothing left over. It answers the question every awakened conscience actually asks. Not can He save? but can He save all the way, and keep saving? The clause that follows supplies the ground: He ever liveth. The salvation is uttermost because the Priest is undying. This is the confessional doctrine of perseverance compressed into one adverb. Christ does not save a man to a point and then hand him back to himself. He saves to the uttermost, because His intercession never lapses and the Father never refuses the Son.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines UTTERMOST as extreme; being in the furthest, greatest or highest degree. As a noun it is the greatest, the utmost extent. Webster marks it the superlative of utter and interchangeable with utmost.

expand to see more

UTTERMOST, a. [utter and most.] — Extreme; being in the furthest, greatest or highest degree; as the uttermost extent or end. UTTERMOST, n. — The greatest; the utmost extent or degree.

Webster keeps the word quantitative, not decorative. Uttermost never means very. It means as far as the thing can go, which is precisely why Hebrews 7:25 uses it of salvation and not of sentiment.

Key Scripture

Hebrews 7:25 — "Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them."

Psalm 2:8 — "Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession."

Acts 1:8 — "But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth."

1 Thessalonians 2:16 — "Forbidding us to speak to the Gentiles that they might be saved, to fill up their sins alway: for the wrath is come upon them to the uttermost."

Modern Corruption

Uttermost is corrupted when Hebrews 7:25 is read as an offer of salvation’s availability rather than a statement of its completeness — making Christ able to save anyone partway rather than able to save His own the whole way.

expand to see more

The common evangelical reduction turns able to save to the uttermost into able to save even the worst sinner. That is true, but it is not what the verse says, and the substitution costs the reader the doctrine. The adverb does not modify the sinner’s badness; it modifies the salvation’s extent. Christ saves completely, finally, to the end. Read the second half of the verse and the point is unmistakable: the reason He saves to the uttermost is that He ever liveth to make intercession. The permanence of the priesthood is the ground of the permanence of the salvation. Strip out the adverb’s real force and Hebrews 7 stops being an argument about the superiority of Melchizedek’s order and becomes a bare invitation.

The second corruption runs the other direction. Where uttermost is used of wrath — the wrath is come upon them to the uttermost (1 Thessalonians 2:16) — the modern instinct is to soften it into a temporary corrective, a chastening that must eventually exhaust itself. That is Origen’s error revived, and every historic Christian confession rejects it. The same word that measures the completeness of salvation measures the completeness of judgment. A reader who wants the full comfort of Hebrews 7:25 must accept that the Authorized Version means the whole distance in both directions.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Two Greek words and two Hebrew words carry uttermost in the Authorized Version, and they divide cleanly between degree and distance. The degree words stand behind the doctrine of perseverance; the distance words stand behind the Great Commission.

expand to see more

Greek pantelēs (G3838) — complete, perfect, to the very end (Hebrews 7:25, save them to the uttermost). Degree, not distance.

Greek eschatos (G2078) — last, farthest, extreme (Acts 1:8, the uttermost part of the earth). Distance, not degree.

Greek telos (G5056) — end, completion, the appointed finish (1 Thessalonians 2:16, to the uttermost, of wrath run out to its term).

Hebrew ephes (H657) — end, extremity, the place where there is nothing further (Psalm 2:8, the uttermost parts of the earth).

Usage

"Christ saves to the uttermost because He ever liveth (Hebrews 7:25) — the permanence of the Priest is the ground of the permanence of the salvation."

"The Father’s promise to the Son reaches the uttermost parts of the earth (Psalm 2:8); the Son’s commission to the church reaches the same edge (Acts 1:8)."

"Wrath also has an uttermost (1 Thessalonians 2:16). The word measures the whole distance in both directions, or it measures nothing."
